meta.titre: Earthquakes and Seismic Waves: from the focus to the seismogram
meta.sous_theme: Seismic waves, instruments and earthquake measurement

sections.contenu_markdown: Most of Cameroon lies far from a plate boundary, so strong earthquakes are rare here, yet sensitive instruments anywhere on Earth record shocks that began thousands of kilometres away. The wiggly trace they produce is the main tool geologists have used to map the inside of the planet. At Advanced Level, questions ask you to separate terms that sound alike (focus and epicentre, body and surface waves, the instrument and its record), to explain how an instrument detects ground motion, and sometimes to turn arrival times into a distance. A clear, well-ordered answer earns most of the marks.

items: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter, and speed equals distance divided by time.
Plates move past, towards or away from each other at transform, convergent and divergent boundaries.
The Earth has a solid crust, a mantle and a core whose outer part is liquid.
On a logarithmic scale, each step up multiplies the quantity by a fixed factor.

sections.titre: Earthquake terms, seismic waves, the seismograph and measurement
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Origin of an earthquake
An earthquake is a sudden release of stored elastic energy in rock, felt as ground shaking. Rock near a fault is slowly strained and bends elastically; when the stress exceeds the strength of the rock or the friction on the fault, it ruptures and springs back (**elastic rebound**). The **focus** (hypocentre) is the point inside the Earth where the rupture starts; the **epicentre** is the point on the surface vertically above it. Foci are classed as shallow (0 to 70 km), intermediate (70 to 300 km) or deep (300 to about 700 km). Most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries, in the Circum-Pacific belt, along the mid-ocean ridges and in the Alpine-Himalayan belt; a few are linked to volcanic activity or to human activity such as filling large reservoirs.

### Seismic waves
| Wave | Group | Particle motion | Travels through | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P (primary) | body, compressional | push and pull, parallel to the direction of travel | solids, liquids and gases | fastest, arrives first |
| S (secondary) | body, shear | sideways or up and down, perpendicular to the direction of travel | solids only | slower than P |
| Love | surface | horizontal shaking, perpendicular to the direction of travel | near the surface only | slower than body waves |
| Rayleigh | surface | rolling elliptical motion in a vertical plane along the direction of travel | near the surface only | usually the slowest |

Body waves pass through the interior and are refracted at boundaries; surface waves travel along the ground, have the largest amplitude and do the most damage.

### Seismograph and seismogram
A **seismograph** is the instrument; a **seismogram** is the record it makes. In a seismometer for vertical motion, a heavy mass hangs from a spring attached to a frame fixed to bedrock. When the ground moves, the frame moves with it, but the inertia of the mass keeps it almost still, so the relative movement of mass and frame is the ground motion. It is recorded by a pen on a rotating drum or, in modern instruments, by a coil on the mass moving in the field of a magnet on the frame; the induced e.m.f. is amplified and digitised. A damper (dashpot) stops the mass oscillating freely. In a labelled sketch name: bedrock or concrete pier, frame, spring, mass, damper, and the recording device.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you are given P and S arrival times, or the S-P interval, and asked for a distance or an origin time.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Because P waves travel faster than S waves, the gap between their arrivals grows with distance. For constant average speeds $v_P$ and $v_S$ over a path of length $d$:

$$t_S - t_P = d\left(\frac{1}{v_S} - \frac{1}{v_P}\right) \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \frac{t_S - t_P}{\dfrac{1}{v_S} - \dfrac{1}{v_P}}$$

One station gives only a distance, so the epicentre lies somewhere on a circle of that radius around the station. Circles drawn from **three** stations intersect at one point, the epicentre (triangulation). The origin time is the P arrival time minus $d/v_P$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks you to compare two earthquakes, or to explain why damage differs between places.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Magnitude** measures the energy released at the source and has one value per earthquake. On the Richter scale it comes from the largest recorded wave amplitude, and it is logarithmic: one whole unit means ten times the amplitude and about $10^{1.5} \approx 32$ times the energy. Two units mean $10^2 = 100$ times the amplitude and $10^3 = 1000$ times the energy. Modern work often uses the moment magnitude, with the same logarithmic idea.

**Intensity** describes the effects on people, buildings and the ground at a particular place, on the Mercalli scale (Roman numerals I to XII). It varies with distance from the epicentre, depth of focus, local ground (soft sediments shake more than solid rock) and quality of construction.

variantes.nom: Seismic waves as evidence for the Earth's interior
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must explain how earthquake waves show that the outer core is liquid or that the Earth is layered.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Waves are refracted or reflected where the rock properties change, and the speeds of P and S waves depend on density and rigidity. Two observations are decisive:

- **S waves are not transmitted through the outer core.** Shear waves cannot travel through a liquid, so stations on the far side of the Earth record no S waves: the outer core is liquid.
- **P-wave shadow zone.** P waves are refracted sharply at the core-mantle boundary, so a ring-shaped zone between about $103^\circ$ and $142^\circ$ from the epicentre receives no direct P waves.

Sudden changes in wave speed at certain depths also locate the main boundaries (Moho, Gutenberg discontinuity).

sections.enonce_markdown: A seismograph record shows the first P wave arriving at 14:20:05 and the first S wave arriving at 14:20:38. Assume constant average speeds of $7.0\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for P waves and $4.0\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for S waves. (a) Calculate the distance from the station to the focus. (b) Find the time at which the earthquake occurred. (c) Explain why a single station cannot give the position of the epicentre.

etapes.action: Identify the arrivals and the interval.
etapes.justification: P waves are faster, so the first arrival is P; the S-P interval is the difference of the two clock times.

etapes.action: Write the relation between interval and distance.
etapes.justification: Both waves cover the same distance $d$ at different speeds, so the interval is $d/v_S - d/v_P$.
Work in seconds and kilometres so the units cancel to km.

etapes.action: Find the travel time of the P wave.
etapes.justification: The P wave left the focus at the origin time, so origin time equals arrival time minus travel time.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $t_P = \dfrac{308}{7.0} = 44\ \mathrm{s}$, so the earthquake occurred 44 s before 14:20:05, that is at 14:19:21

etapes.justification: A second path to the same answer confirms the arithmetic.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $t_S = \dfrac{308}{4.0} = 77\ \mathrm{s}$, and 77 s after 14:19:21 is 14:20:38, as recorded

etapes.action: Explain the limit of one station.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The epicentre can lie anywhere on a circle of radius 308 km centred on the station; records from at least three stations give three circles that intersect at one point.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) The focus is **308 km** from the station (the epicentral distance is slightly smaller if the focus is deep). (b) The earthquake occurred at **14:19:21**. (c) One station fixes only a distance, so **three stations** are needed to locate the epicentre by triangulation.

items.erreur_markdown: The epicentre is the point underground where the earthquake begins.
items.pourquoi_faux: That point is the focus (hypocentre). The epicentre is on the surface.
items.correction_markdown: The **focus** is the point inside the Earth where rupture starts; the **epicentre** is the point on the surface directly above the focus.

items.erreur_markdown: P waves are transverse waves, so the rock moves up and down as they pass.
items.pourquoi_faux: P waves are compressional: the particles move back and forth parallel to the direction of travel, alternately squeezing and stretching the rock.
items.correction_markdown: **P waves** are longitudinal (compressional); **S waves** and Love waves are transverse (shear).

items.erreur_markdown: The seismogram is the instrument that detects ground movement.
items.pourquoi_faux: The instrument is the seismograph (or seismometer). The seismogram is the paper or digital record of the shaking.
items.correction_markdown: Seismograph = instrument. Seismogram = record of ground motion against time.

items.erreur_markdown: A magnitude 7 earthquake is only a little stronger than a magnitude 6 earthquake, about 7/6 as strong.
items.pourquoi_faux: The scale is logarithmic. A rise of one unit multiplies the recorded amplitude by 10 and the energy by about 32.
items.correction_markdown: Magnitude 7 gives ten times the amplitude and about **32 times** the energy of magnitude 6.

items.erreur_markdown: S waves cannot pass through the mantle because it is liquid.
items.pourquoi_faux: The mantle is solid rock, so S waves do cross it. They are stopped only by the liquid outer core.
items.correction_markdown: S waves travel through the **solid mantle** but not through the **liquid outer core**; this is the evidence that the outer core is liquid.

items.enonce_markdown: State three differences between P waves and S waves. (3 marks)
items.solution_markdown:
Award a mark for each correct difference, for example:

1. P waves are compressional (particles move parallel to the direction of travel); S waves are shear waves (particles move perpendicular to it).
2. P waves travel through solids, liquids and gases; S waves travel through solids only.
3. P waves are faster and arrive first; S waves are slower and arrive second.

Other acceptable points: P waves can be refracted into the outer core while S waves cannot enter it. **Three correct, comparative differences earn 3 marks**; a statement about one wave only earns no mark.

items.enonce_markdown: Two stations X and Y record the same earthquake. The average speeds are $6.0\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for P waves and $3.6\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for S waves. The S-P interval is 18 s at X and 30 s at Y. (a) Calculate the distance from each station to the focus. (b) State which station is nearer. (c) For station Y, calculate the time after the earthquake at which the S wave arrives.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\dfrac{1}{3.6} - \dfrac{1}{6.0} = \dfrac{1}{9}\ \mathrm{s\,km^{-1}}$, so $d = 9 \times \text{interval}$.

X: $d = 9 \times 18 = 162\ \mathrm{km}$. Y: $d = 9 \times 30 = 270\ \mathrm{km}$.

(b) X is nearer, because a shorter S-P interval means a shorter distance.

(c) Travel time of the S wave to Y: $t_S = \dfrac{270}{3.6} = 75\ \mathrm{s}$. Check: the P wave takes $270/6.0 = 45\ \mathrm{s}$, and $75 - 45 = 30\ \mathrm{s}$, equal to the interval.

**X: 162 km; Y: 270 km; X is nearer; S wave reaches Y 75 s after the earthquake.**

items.enonce_markdown: Earthquake A has magnitude 5.2 and earthquake B has magnitude 7.2 on the Richter scale. (a) Calculate how many times larger the recorded amplitude of B is than that of A. (b) Calculate how many times more energy B releases, taking one magnitude unit as a factor of 32 in energy (that is, $10^{1.5}$). (c) Explain why the intensity of the same earthquake can differ between two towns. (d) Explain why the heavy mass of a vertical seismometer stays almost stationary while the ground moves.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The difference is $7.2 - 5.2 = 2.0$ units, so the amplitude ratio is $10^{2.0} = 100$.

(b) Energy ratio $= (10^{1.5})^{2.0} = 10^{3} = 1000$. **B records 100 times the amplitude and releases about 1000 times the energy.**

(c) Intensity measures effects at a place. It depends on distance from the epicentre, depth of the focus, the type of ground (loose, water-saturated sediments amplify shaking, solid rock does not) and the strength of buildings, so two towns at different distances or on different ground are shaken differently, while the magnitude has a single value.

(d) The mass has inertia. It is joined to the frame only by a spring, which transmits little force to it when the frame moves quickly, so the mass stays nearly at rest in space. The frame, fixed to the ground, moves relative to it, and this relative movement is what the pen or coil records.

items_markdown: The **focus** is where rupture starts underground; the **epicentre** is the surface point directly above it.
P waves are compressional, fastest, and pass through solids, liquids and gases; S waves are shear waves and pass through solids only; surface waves (Love, Rayleigh) are slowest and most destructive.
A **seismograph** is the instrument (mass, spring, frame, damper, recorder); a **seismogram** is the record. The mass stays still because of its inertia.
Distance from one station is found from the S-P interval, $d = (t_S - t_P)/(1/v_S - 1/v_P)$; three stations fix the epicentre.
Magnitude (logarithmic, energy at source) differs from intensity (effects at a place). One magnitude unit is about 10 times the amplitude and 32 times the energy.
No S waves through the outer core and a P-wave shadow zone between about 103 and 142 degrees show that the outer core is liquid.
